stops.note: 'married woman', from mater 'mother'; the Matronalia festival on 1 March honoured Rome's matrons
from Latin via Greek Matrona, a saint's name in the Orthodox calendar; it became so common among peasants that it evoked a stout country mother
'little Matryona'; the first set was carved by Vasily Zvyozdochkin and painted by Sergey Malyutin around 1890 at the Abramtsevo craft colony, reportedly inspired by a Japanese nesting doll
the dolls won a medal at the 1900 Paris Exposition Universelle, launching their export

current_meaning: a set of wooden Russian dolls of decreasing size nested inside each other
